chunks: "The core idea is one voltage loop that decides how much total current the load needs, plus a PWM generator that splits that into N staggered pulses, one per phase.
Each phase is a normal buck stage with its own inductor, and the currents add at the output. The main challenge is current sharing.
The phases are connected through a very low impedance, only a few milliohms, so a tiny difference in duty cycle, in on-resistance or in inductor DCR makes a large difference in current.
If you gave one phase 0. 1 percent more duty at 12 volts with about 4 milliohms in the loop, that is roughly 3 amps of imbalance, on a 15 amp phase.
So the controller senses each phase current, usually through the inductor DCR or the power stage, compares it with the average, and trims each phase's duty until they match.
That brings the next problems: the sense signal is small, a few millivolts, so offset and temperature drift show up directly as imbalance.
DCR sensing needs temperature compensation. Layout has to be symmetric so no phase has extra resistance or thermal advantage. Then there are dynamic issues.
During a load step you want all phases on together. At light load you shed phases to save power, and adding them back changes loop gain and ripple.
And the control loop has to be stable with the combined L over N plant.
So it is more parts, more control, more layout care, in exchange for current, ripple and transient performance."
